Sparse matrices stored in Zarr with ZarrSparseMatrix

Gabriel Hoffman

2026-10-30

Source: vignettes/ZarrSparseMatrix.Rmd
ZarrSparseMatrix.Rmd

Introduction

Large sparse matrices, such as single-cell counts, are often stored in Zarr stores. AnnData’s write_zarr() saves its X matrix in a Zarr group as three 1D arrays:

  • data: the nonzero values
  • indices: the 0-based column (CSR) or row (CSC) index of each value
  • indptr: where each row (CSR) or column (CSC) starts in data and indices

ZarrSparseMatrix represents such a matrix in R without loading it into memory. It is a DelayedMatrix, so it works with any code written for DelayedArray objects, and it is the Zarr counterpart of HDF5Array::H5SparseMatrix. Data is read with Rarr only when it is needed. Selecting rows of a CSR matrix, or columns of a CSC matrix, reads only the corresponding parts of data and indices.

Installation 

if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly=TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

# Install from Bioconductor
BiocManager::install("ZarrSparseMatrix")

# Install from GitHub
# remotes::install_github("GabrielHoffman/ZarrSparseMatrix")

Creating a ZarrSparseMatrix

The package includes a small example store: simulated counts for 200 cells and 100 genes, stored like AnnData’s X (CSR layout, cells as rows). exampleZarr() unzips it to a temporary directory and returns its path.

suppressMessages({
library(ZarrSparseMatrix)
})

store <- exampleZarr()
store
#> [1] "/var/folders/7_/sqg9z3y97xd51lj4lml82n2w0000gn/T//RtmppvXtZi/ZarrSparseMatrix-example/example.zarr"
list.files(store, recursive=TRUE, all.files=TRUE)[1:6]
#> [1] ".zgroup"        "X/.zattrs"      "X/.zgroup"      "X/data/.zarray"
#> [5] "X/data/0"       "X/data/1"

Pass the path to the store and the name of the group:

X <- ZarrSparseMatrix(store, "X")
X
#> <200 x 100> sparse ZarrSparseMatrix object of type "integer":
#>          [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4] ...  [,97]  [,98]  [,99] [,100]
#>   [1,]     11      0      0      1   .      0      0      0      1
#>   [2,]      1      0      0      2   .      0      0      0      0
#>   [3,]      0      0      2      2   .      0      0      0      0
#>   [4,]      0      0      0      1   .      0      0      2      0
#>   [5,]      0      0      1      1   .      0      0      2      0
#>    ...      .      .      .      .   .      .      .      .      .
#> [196,]      1      1      1      0   .      0      0      0      0
#> [197,]      5      0      1      1   .      0      0      0      2
#> [198,]      1      0      0      2   .      0      0      0      0
#> [199,]      4      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      0
#> [200,]      0      0      0      3   .      0      0      0      0

The dimensions and layout come from the group’s shape and encoding-type attributes:

dim(X)
#> [1] 200 100
type(X)
#> [1] "integer"
is_sparse(X)
#> [1] TRUE
seed(X)
#> <200 x 100> sparse CSR_ZarrSparseMatrixSeed object of type "integer":
#> # dirname: /private/var/folders/7_/sqg9z3y97xd51lj4lml82n2w0000gn/T/RtmppvXtZi/ZarrSparseMatrix-example
#> # basename: example.zarr
#> # group: X

nzcount() gives the number of stored values, read from the metadata of the data array:

nzcount(seed(X))
#> [1] 6090
nzcount(seed(X)) / length(X)
#> [1] 0.3045

Subsetting

Subsetting is delayed. Data is read when the result is printed or realized:

X[1:5, 1:8]
#> <5 x 8> sparse DelayedMatrix object of type "integer":
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7] [,8]
#> [1,]   11    0    0    1    0    0    0    0
#> [2,]    1    0    0    2    1    3    0    0
#> [3,]    0    0    2    2    0    3    0    0
#> [4,]    0    0    0    1    2    0    1    0
#> [5,]    0    0    1    1    0    1    0    3
as.matrix(X[c(10, 3, 3), c(100, 1)])
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]    1    2
#> [2,]    0    0
#> [3,]    0    0

Bioconductor usually stores genes as rows and cells as columns, which is the transpose of AnnData. t(X) gives a delayed transpose. Transposing the seed instead turns the CSR seed into a CSC seed without reading any data, and gives a ZarrSparseMatrix with genes as rows:

t(X)
#> <100 x 200> sparse DelayedMatrix object of type "integer":
#>          [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4] ... [,197] [,198] [,199] [,200]
#>   [1,]     11      1      0      0   .      5      1      4      0
#>   [2,]      0      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      0
#>   [3,]      0      0      2      0   .      1      0      0      0
#>   [4,]      1      2      2      1   .      1      2      0      3
#>   [5,]      0      1      0      2   .      0      1      0      0
#>    ...      .      .      .      .   .      .      .      .      .
#>  [96,]      0      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      2
#>  [97,]      0      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      0
#>  [98,]      0      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      0
#>  [99,]      0      0      0      2   .      0      0      0      0
#> [100,]      1      0      0      0   .      2      0      0      0

tX <- ZarrSparseMatrix(t(seed(X)))
tX
#> <100 x 200> sparse ZarrSparseMatrix object of type "integer":
#>          [,1]   [,2]   [,3]   [,4] ... [,197] [,198] [,199] [,200]
#>   [1,]     11      1      0      0   .      5      1      4      0
#>   [2,]      0      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      0
#>   [3,]      0      0      2      0   .      1      0      0      0
#>   [4,]      1      2      2      1   .      1      2      0      3
#>   [5,]      0      1      0      2   .      0      1      0      0
#>    ...      .      .      .      .   .      .      .      .      .
#>  [96,]      0      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      2
#>  [97,]      0      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      0
#>  [98,]      0      0      0      0   .      0      0      0      0
#>  [99,]      0      0      0      2   .      0      0      0      0
#> [100,]      1      0      0      0   .      2      0      0      0
seed(tX)
#> <100 x 200> sparse CSC_ZarrSparseMatrixSeed object of type "integer":
#> # dirname: /private/var/folders/7_/sqg9z3y97xd51lj4lml82n2w0000gn/T/RtmppvXtZi/ZarrSparseMatrix-example
#> # basename: example.zarr
#> # group: X

Summaries and block processing

Summaries such as rowSums() and colSums() are computed block by block, so only one block is in memory at a time:

libsize <- rowSums(X)
head(libsize)
#> [1] 128 143 122 123  98 118

gene_mean <- colMeans(X)
head(gene_mean)
#> [1] 2.390 0.205 0.715 1.210 0.645 0.380

The block size is set with setAutoBlockSize(). A small value forces many blocks, which shows that the result doesn’t depend on it:

old <- getAutoBlockSize()
setAutoBlockSize(2000)
#> automatic block size set to 2000 bytes (was 1e+08)
all.equal(colSums(X), colSums(as.matrix(X)))
#> [1] TRUE
setAutoBlockSize(old)
#> automatic block size set to 1e+08 bytes (was 2000)

Operations such as normalization and log1p() are delayed too. Nothing is computed until the result is used:

logcounts <- log1p(X / libsize * 1e4)
logcounts
#> <200 x 100> sparse DelayedMatrix object of type "double":
#>            [,1]     [,2]     [,3] ...    [,99]   [,100]
#>   [1,] 6.757368 0.000000 0.000000   . 0.000000 4.371029
#>   [2,] 4.261694 0.000000 0.000000   . 0.000000 0.000000
#>   [3,] 0.000000 0.000000 5.105548   . 0.000000 0.000000
#>   [4,] 0.000000 0.000000 0.000000   . 5.097434 0.000000
#>   [5,] 0.000000 0.000000 4.635125   . 5.323408 0.000000
#>    ...        .        .        .   .        .        .
#> [196,] 5.042432 5.042432 5.042432   . 0.000000 0.000000
#> [197,] 6.257348 0.000000 4.655546   . 0.000000 5.343928
#> [198,] 4.386580 0.000000 0.000000   . 0.000000 0.000000
#> [199,] 6.014114 0.000000 0.000000   . 0.000000 0.000000
#> [200,] 0.000000 0.000000 0.000000   . 0.000000 0.000000
showtree(logcounts)
#> 200x100 double, sparse: DelayedMatrix object
#> └─ 200x100 double, sparse: Stack of 2 unary iso op(s)
#>    └─ 200x100 double, sparse: Unary iso op with args
#>       └─ 200x100 integer, sparse: [seed] CSR_ZarrSparseMatrixSeed object

blockApply() runs your own function on each block. Here, the number of nonzero values per block of rows:

grid <- rowAutoGrid(X, nrow=50)
unlist(blockApply(X, function(block) nzcount(block), grid=grid,
                  as.sparse=TRUE))
#> [1] 1562 1518 1518 1492

Converting to in-memory matrices

as() loads the matrix into memory as any sparse or dense class:

m <- as(X, "dgCMatrix")
class(m)
#> [1] "dgCMatrix"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "Matrix"

svt <- as(X, "SVT_SparseArray")
class(svt)
#> [1] "SVT_SparseMatrix"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "SparseArray"

dense <- as.matrix(X[1:3, 1:3])
dense
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]   11    0    0
#> [2,]    1    0    0
#> [3,]    0    0    2

Row and column names

AnnData stores cell and gene names separately (in obs and var), so the names aren’t in the X group. Pass them with the dimnames argument:

cells <- sprintf("cell_%03d", seq_len(nrow(X)))
genes <- sprintf("gene_%03d", seq_len(ncol(X)))
X <- ZarrSparseMatrix(store, "X", dimnames=list(cells, genes))
X[1:3, 1:4]
#> <3 x 4> sparse DelayedMatrix object of type "integer":
#>          gene_001 gene_002 gene_003 gene_004
#> cell_001       11        0        0        1
#> cell_002        1        0        0        2
#> cell_003        0        0        2        2

Using a ZarrSparseMatrix in a SingleCellExperiment

A ZarrSparseMatrix can be used as an assay, and stays on disk:

suppressMessages({
library(SingleCellExperiment)
})

counts <- ZarrSparseMatrix(t(seed(X)))
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays=list(counts=counts))
sce
#> class: SingleCellExperiment 
#> dim: 100 200 
#> metadata(0):
#> assays(1): counts
#> rownames(100): gene_001 gene_002 ... gene_099 gene_100
#> rowData names(0):
#> colnames(200): cell_001 cell_002 ... cell_199 cell_200
#> colData names(0):
#> reducedDimNames(0):
#> mainExpName: NULL
#> altExpNames(0):
class(counts(sce))
#> [1] "ZarrSparseMatrix"
#> attr(,"package")
#> [1] "ZarrSparseMatrix"

CSC matrices and overriding the metadata

A CSC matrix (encoding-type csc_matrix) is read the same way. Selecting columns of a CSC matrix is cheap, and selecting rows of a CSR matrix is cheap.

If the group has no shape or encoding-type attribute, give them with dim and sparse.layout. For example, reading the CSR X above as CSC with reversed dimensions gives its transpose directly:

Xcsc <- ZarrSparseMatrix(store, "X", dim=rev(dim(X)), sparse.layout="CSC")
seed(Xcsc)
#> <100 x 200> sparse CSC_ZarrSparseMatrixSeed object of type "integer":
#> # dirname: /private/var/folders/7_/sqg9z3y97xd51lj4lml82n2w0000gn/T/RtmppvXtZi/ZarrSparseMatrix-example
#> # basename: example.zarr
#> # group: X
all.equal(as.matrix(Xcsc), t(as.matrix(X)), check.attributes=FALSE)
#> [1] TRUE

To read an alternative array that shares indices and indptr with data, pass its name as subdata.

Writing a Zarr store from Python

Use Zarr format 2, because Rarr reads Zarr v2 arrays. Recent versions of anndata warn that the default will change to v3. Setting the format explicitly keeps your stores readable in R:

import anndata as ad
import scanpy as sc

ad.settings.zarr_write_format = 2

adata = sc.datasets.pbmc3k()
adata.write_zarr("pbmc3k.zarr")

Then in R:

X <- ZarrSparseMatrix("pbmc3k.zarr", "X")
